title: Grounding Driving VLA via Inverse Kinematics
claim: Existing models keep their output unchanged when the input gains a critical hazard; ours reacts to it, showing real use of the input.
layout: 3 rows by 6 columns, left-to-right, original vs. modified input, per-method outputs
description: The figure is a grid with three rows, each a different driving scene (night, daytime street, rainy road). The first column is the original front-camera image. The second column is the same image with a large gray sedan stitched in directly ahead of the ego vehicle. The four right columns are narrow bird's-eye-view trajectory plots, labeled Alpamayo, Imp.-VLA, Open.VLA and Ours, with Ours in bold. Each plot has a dark ego-vehicle box at the bottom, a green line for the trajectory before stitching and a red line for the trajectory after. In the three baseline columns, red and green lines almost overlap and run straight ahead. In the Ours column, the red path is much shorter and curves, showing slowdown or avoidance. The eye goes to the stitched car and then to the contrast in the last column.
caption: Counterfactual obstacle stitching on nuScenes val. Left columns: original front-camera image and the same image with a near-range vehicle sprite stitched in front of the ego. Right columns: BEV trajectories before (green) and after (red) stitching for existing VLAs and our model. While existing VLAs' trajectory remains nearly invariant to the visual input, our model produces a distinct slowdown/avoidance reaction in response to the stitched obstacle, demonstrating that visual features causally influence its trajectory output.
abstract: Counterfactual obstacle insertion exposes blind planning in representative Driving VLAs: their trajectories remain largely unchanged despite a vehicle appearing directly ahead. An empirically calibrated bias-variance analysis identifies how ego-predictable training examples admit a shortcut through ego status and commands. We address this failure with an inverse-kinematics-inspired architecture that anchors trajectory decoding on current and predicted future visual states. First, a next visual state prediction objective that requires the LLM to predict the future visual scene provides dense visual supervision and suppresses shortcut paths. Second, a separate Inverse Kinematics Network (a cross-attention-based conditional diffusion model) that takes only the current and future visual states as input is designed to suppress reliance on ego status and textual shortcuts during trajectory decoding. Our 0.5B model achieves state-of-the-art trajectory planning performance on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and nuScenes using cameras alone, without LiDAR or a BEV encoder. Against the matched OpenDriveVLA* baseline, it improves NAVSIM PDMS and EPDMS by 19.0 and 20.4 points, respectively. Controlled ablations and intervention analyses support improved use of visual features, with future-state prediction sharpening hazard-specific responses.
